extracted.intended_audience: students, clergy, and scholars of Catholic dogmatic theology
extracted.subtask_description: A dogmatic-theology treatment defining and systematizing the concept of divine grace (actual and habitual) within Catholic tradition, including distinctions, divisions, and theological criteria. Intended as a reference for theological study and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: General notion of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace (gratia, χάρις) is a word of wide reach used in several senses; dogmatic theology is concerned with the fundamental meaning of grace as 'a free gift or favor' (donum gratis datum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author enumerates four reducible meanings: (a) benevolence shown by a superior to an inferior, (b) an objective favor/free gift, (c) personal charm/attractiveness, (d) thanksgiving. He stresses that the first/fundamental meaning is a free gratuitous gift and that dogmatic theology uses the term in this fundamental sense. Example citations: St. Paul and St. Augustine on grace as 'something gratuitously given.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural vs supernatural grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes purely natural gifts (creation, health, talents) from supernatural graces; in the dogmatic sense 'grace' denotes a gratuitous supernatural gift that ontologically exceeds nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how Scripture and Fathers sometimes use 'grace' for natural favors but that dogmatic theology reserves the term for supernatural gifts (both preternatural and strictly supernatural). Derives definition 'Grace is a gratuitous super-natural gift.' Discusses negative and positive undeservedness and cites Augustine and councils to justify the distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace of God vs grace of Christ
rubrics_metrics.description: A secondary/accidental distinction: 'gratia Dei' (from divine benevolence) vs 'gratia Christi' (derived from the merits of Christ); both are supernatural graces but differ in accent and causal origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides criteria to distinguish them: (A) degree of recipient's unworthiness (non_dignus vs indignus), (B) elevating vs healing function (gratia elevans vs elevans simul et sanans), (C) relation to merits of Christ. Notes Thomist and Scotist positions and concludes the dogmatic treatise concerns grace derived from the merits of Jesus Christ; refines definition accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: External vs internal grace
rubrics_metrics.description: External grace (gratia externa) comprises supernatural institutions that stimulate pious thoughts (Scripture, Church, Sacraments); internal grace (gratia interna) operates invisibly in the soul and places it in relation to God as supernatural end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the treatise concerns internal grace. Explains that external grace is generally a preparation for internal grace and cites St. Paul distinguishing 'law' and 'faith'. Gives examples (Bible, sacraments) and argues internal grace aims at sanctification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratia gratis data vs gratia gratum faciens
rubrics_metrics.description: Two species of internal grace: gratia gratum faciens (ingratiating, intended for salvation/holiness of all) and gratia gratis data (graces freely given for sanctification of others, e.g., charismata, ordinary priestly powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the difference in scope (gratum faciens intended for all; gratis data bestowed on a few). Argues gratum faciens is intrinsically superior; cites St. Paul and the primacy of charity. Notes that gratia gratis data is treated elsewhere (Apologetics, Mystic and Sacramental Theology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual vs habitual (sanctifying) grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction: actual grace is a transient supernatural help enabling salutary acts; habitual (sanctifying) grace is a more enduring state or habit rendering men pleasing to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines actual grace as an unmerited, supernatural, internal divine help, based on merits of Jesus Christ, rendering man pleasing to God and enabling salutary acts. States actual grace tends either to produce or to preserve/increase sanctifying grace, and is therefore a means while sanctifying grace is the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold causality of actual grace (moral and physical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual grace exercises both a moral causality (removing obstacles, inspiring delight in virtue and hatred of sin) and a physical causality (elevating the faculties of the soul to perform supernatural acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues moral causality addresses will's weakness (concupiscence) and can sometimes deprive will of freedom to resist (e.g., Paul's conversion). Physical causality is metaphysical necessity: nature alone cannot perform salutary acts; grace 'elevates' faculties. Cites Perrone's classic definition and scriptural/traditional support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of actual grace by faculties and will (illuminating/strengthening/sensitive; prevenient vs efficacious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual grace can be classified according to the human faculties (intellect, will, sensitive faculties) and with respect to the will's freedom as prevenient/coöperating, efficacious, or merely sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies illuminating grace of the intellect, strengthening grace of the will, and graces affecting the sensitive sphere. Notes prevenient (coöperating) vs efficacious (or merely sufficient) distinctions with respect to free consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illuminating grace of the intellect (mediate vs immediate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illuminating grace (gratia illuminationis) inspires salutary thoughts in the intellect and may be mediate (via natural/external means like sermons, Scripture) or immediate (direct supernatural enlightenment by the Holy Ghost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides scriptural (1 Cor. III; Paul's metaphors) and patristic (Augustine) arguments for the necessity of immediate illumination. Explains mediate illumination prepares for immediate illumination, and discusses psychological and pedagogical aspects (external aids elicit salutary thoughts but increase depends on God).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthening grace of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratia inspirationis (strengthening grace) produces pious affections and wholesome resolutions; like illumination it may be mediate or immediate, but its immediate operation on the will is deemed indispensable for salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from Tradition (Augustine) and the Council of Carthage (A.D. 418) that grace must not only reveal what to do but grant the desire and power to do it. Discusses emotions/passions as manifestations and distinguishes knowledge from charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual graces of the sensitive sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual grace likely influences the sensitive faculties (imagination, appetitus sensitivus), exciting phantasms corresponding to supernatural thoughts or paralyzing concupiscence, aiding or hindering salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes probability rather than certainty; appeals to the composite nature of man (body and soul) and Aristotle's claim that mind cannot think without imagination. Gives examples (spiritual joy manifesting in sensitive appetite) and cites Augustine on delectatio victrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illuminating and strengthening graces as vital acts; 'fluent qualities' debate
rubrics_metrics.description: The illuminating and strengthening graces are essentially vital acts of intellect and will (judgments, apprehensions, emotions). Some Thomists add preceding extrinsic non-vital 'fluent' qualities (potentia obœdientialis) as real graces required to produce vital acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the view that vital supernatural acts are produced by preceding non-vital supernatural powers; notes controversy and opponents' ironic label of such qualities as 'dead.' Cites Augustine and Aquinas on how internal acts manifest and the Aristotelian axiom 'actus moventis in moto est motus.'
